chapters.title: Origins & the medical calling
chapters.question: What shaped the student before the national hero?

roles.calamba: Calamba, Laguna: birthplace and early education
roles.gomburza: Gómez, Burgos and Zamora, executed in 1872
roles.medical-lens: Ophthalmology: the medical specialty concerned with the eye

chapters.narration: Begin with the person, not the monument. Rizal was born in Calamba in 1861, and his mother Teodora was his first teacher. The execution of Gómez, Burgos and Zamora in 1872 belongs to the colonial world in which he grew up. His mother’s failing eyesight helped motivate his interest in ophthalmology, the study and treatment of eye disease. He continued medical study in Europe.

Ophthalmology means the study and treatment of the eye.

chapters.title: The European journey
chapters.question: How did study abroad become a printed argument?

roles.education-route: Selected journey from Manila to Madrid and European medical training
roles.noli-printing: Noli Me Tangere, printed in Berlin in 1887

chapters.narration: In 1882, Rizal continued his medical studies in Madrid. His European years also included further medical training and writing. Follow two outcomes of the journey: the physician developed a specialist practice, while the writer prepared a novel about colonial society. Noli Me Tangere was published in Berlin in 1887. The route is orientation, not a complete travel log.

chapters.title: Two novels, a public argument
chapters.question: How can fiction make colonial abuses visible?

roles.colonial-abuses: The novels dramatize colonial oppression; the scene is illustrative
roles.readers: Writing reaches readers and discussion, not a measured audience

chapters.narration: Read these as novels with a political purpose. Noli Me Tangere appeared in Berlin in 1887; El Filibusterismo followed in Ghent in 1891. Both dramatized oppression under Spanish colonial rule. Their characters and situations gave readers concrete ways to recognize abuse. The books could influence reformists and revolutionaries without being a military chain of command.

cues.text: Fiction → readers → discussion. Influence is distinct from military command.

chapters.title: La Liga & the Dapitan years
chapters.question: What did reform look like during exile?

roles.la-liga: La Liga Filipina: a civic association founded 3 July 1892
roles.exile-route: Manila to Dapitan, northwestern Mindanao, July 1892
roles.clinic: Rizal continued medical practice in Dapitan
roles.school: Education was part of his work in exile
roles.waterworks: A schematic water channel represents documented waterworks
roles.katipunan: A separate revolutionary organization, not founded by Rizal

chapters.narration: Rizal founded La Liga Filipina in Manila in July 1892. Colonial authorities soon sent him into exile in Dapitan, on northwestern Mindanao. Exile restricted his movement, but it did not end his work. He practiced medicine, taught, studied nature and helped design waterworks. La Liga was a civic association; the Katipunan was a separate revolutionary organization.

chapters.title: Trial, farewell & execution
chapters.question: Why was he executed—and what did his death change?

roles.execution-december: A Spanish military court convicted Rizal; execution on 30 December 1896
roles.chronology-test: August precedes December: his death did not start the revolution
roles.influence: Inspirational influence is distinct from military initiation or command
roles.farewell: The untitled farewell poem later known as Mi Último Adiós

chapters.narration: A Spanish military court convicted Rizal of forming an illicit organization and inciting rebellion. He was executed at Bagumbayan on 30 December 1896. His farewell poem, later known as Mi Último Adiós, survived. Now compare the dates: the Philippine Revolution had already begun in August. His death could inspire people, but it could not begin an uprising already underway.

chapters.title: From a life to public memory
chapters.question: How does a life keep reaching new generations?

roles.legacy-books: Rizal’s writing remains available to new readers
roles.monument: Public commemoration, shown by an illustrative monument
roles.rizal-law: Republic Act 1425, enacted in 1956, requires study of Rizal
roles.contributions: New readers encounter his life and writings through education

chapters.narration: Remembrance is more than a statue. Rizal left writing that later generations could read. Public commemoration made his life a shared symbol, and Republic Act 1425 made study of his life and works part of education. Keep the connections in view: the person produced work, historical events changed its meaning, and institutions carried that memory to new readers.

cues.text: Books preserve the work; monuments mark public remembrance.
Education brings the life and writing to new readers.
